AI Compass

AI glossary: artificial intelligence words in simple language

Every important AI word in one plain sentence, with an everyday example.

Basics

  • Artificial intelligence (AI)Computer systems that can do tasks that usually need human intelligence.
  • AlgorithmA clear, step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem.
  • DataFacts and information a computer can store and use, such as numbers, words, pictures and clicks.
  • DatasetA large, organised collection of examples used to train or test an AI model.
  • ModelA program that has learned patterns from data and uses them to make predictions or create something new.
  • RobotA machine that can sense its surroundings and move or act in the physical world.
  • AutomationUsing machines or software to do tasks by themselves, with little or no human help.
  • Natural language processing (NLP)The area of AI that works with human language: understanding, translating and creating text or speech.
  • Turing testAlan Turing's 1950 test: a machine passes if people chatting with it in text can't reliably tell it from a human.
  • Recommendation systemAn AI system that suggests things you might like, based on what you and similar people chose before.
  • Expert systemAn early kind of AI that makes decisions by following many if-then rules written down by human experts.
  • Collaborative filteringRecommending things that people with tastes like yours enjoyed, without knowing what the things are about.
  • Data cleaningFinding and fixing mistakes in data, such as missing, wrong, repeated or impossible values, before a model learns from it.

Learning

  • Machine learning (ML)A way of building AI in which the computer learns patterns from examples instead of following rules written by a programmer.
  • TrainingThe process in which a model learns from examples by making guesses and correcting its mistakes again and again.
  • Neural networkAn AI model made of many simple connected units (neurons), arranged in layers, that learn patterns together.
  • Artificial neuronThe tiny building block of a neural network: it weighs its input numbers, adds them up and passes a signal on.
  • Deep learningMachine learning with neural networks that have many layers.
  • Parameters (weights)The numbers inside a model that change during training and store what it has learned.
  • Supervised learningLearning from examples that come with the right answers (labels).
  • Unsupervised learningLearning from data without answers, by finding hidden patterns and groups on its own.
  • OverfittingWhen a model memorises its training examples so closely that it does badly on new data.
  • GeneralisationA model's ability to work well on new examples it has never seen, not just on its training data.
  • Loss functionA score that measures how wrong a model's answers are; training tries to make it as small as possible.
  • Gradient descentA way to train a model by changing its parameters, step by step, in the direction that makes the loss smaller.
  • Learning rateA setting that controls how big a step a model takes each time it adjusts its parameters during training.
  • BackpropagationThe method a neural network uses to work out how much each weight was to blame for a mistake.
  • ClusteringGrouping similar things together without being told what the groups are.
  • Evolutionary algorithmA way of solving problems that copies evolution: the best of many tries are kept, mixed and slightly changed, generation after generation.
  • Decision treeA model that answers by asking a chain of yes/no questions about an example, like a flowchart.
  • Naive Bayes classifierA simple model that adds up clues, such as words, each counted separately, to guess a category like “spam”.
  • Test setExamples put aside before training and used only to check how well a model does on data it has never seen.
  • LabelThe right answer attached to a training example, such as “cat” on a photo of a cat.
  • AccuracyThe share of examples a model gets right, usually measured on a test set.
  • False positiveA false alarm: the model says “yes” (spam, sick, danger) when the true answer is “no”.

Computer vision

  • Computer visionThe area of AI that helps computers find and recognise things in photos and videos.
  • PixelOne tiny square of a digital picture, stored as numbers that say how bright it is or what colour it has.
  • ConvolutionSliding a small grid of numbers (a filter) across a picture to find patterns such as edges.
  • Convolutional neural network (CNN)A neural network for pictures whose layers use convolutions to find patterns, from edges up to whole objects.
  • Adversarial exampleAn input changed very slightly, often invisibly to people, so that an AI model makes a mistake.
  • Data augmentationMaking more training examples from the ones you have, for example by flipping, turning or shifting pictures.

Trial and error

  • Reinforcement learningLearning by trial and error: an AI tries actions and gets rewards or penalties for the results.
  • AgentAn AI that acts on its own to reach a goal: it notices what is happening, chooses an action and sees the result.
  • RewardThe score an agent gets after an action, telling it how good the result was.
  • Exploration vs. exploitationThe choice an agent faces between trying something new (exploring) and using what already works (exploiting).
  • Q-learningA reinforcement learning method in which an agent learns a score (a Q-value) for every action in every situation.
  • Reward hackingWhen an AI finds a loophole that earns lots of reward without doing what its designers really wanted.
  • Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)A way to make a chatbot more helpful: people rate its answers, and those ratings become its reward in reinforcement learning.

Language models

  • Large language model (LLM)A huge neural network trained on enormous amounts of text to predict the next token.
  • TokenA small piece of text, such as a word or part of a word, that a language model reads and writes.
  • TransformerA neural network design from 2017 that uses attention to work out how the words of a text relate.
  • Next-token predictionWhat a language model does: it gives every possible next token a probability, picks one, and repeats.
  • AttentionThe part of a transformer that lets each word look at the other words and decide which of them matter for its meaning.
  • TemperatureA setting that controls how predictable or surprising a language model's choice of words is.
  • EmbeddingA list of numbers that stands for a word, picture or other thing, so that similar things get similar numbers.
  • Context windowThe amount of text, measured in tokens, that a language model can take into account at once.
  • Fine-tuningExtra training that takes a model that has already learned a lot and adjusts it for a particular job.
  • Reasoning modelA language model trained to work through a problem step by step before it gives its final answer.

Generative AI

  • Generative AIAI that creates new text, images, music, video or code from patterns it has learned.
  • ChatbotA program you can have a conversation with by typing or speaking.
  • PromptThe instruction or question you give to a generative AI.
  • HallucinationWhen an AI confidently gives an answer that sounds right but is false or made up.
  • Diffusion modelAn image generator that learns to remove noise step by step, turning random speckles into a picture that matches a prompt.
  • Generative adversarial network (GAN)Two neural networks trained against each other: one makes fakes, the other tries to catch them, and both get better.
  • Multimodal AIAI that can work with more than one kind of data, such as text, images and sound, in the same conversation.

Ethics & Safety

  • BiasWhen an AI system treats some people or groups unfairly, often because of unbalanced training data.
  • DeepfakeA fake video, image or voice recording made with AI that shows someone saying or doing something they never did.
  • PrivacyYour right to control your personal information and who can see it.
  • Black boxA system whose inner workings are hard to see or explain, even for the people who built it.
  • Artificial general intelligence (AGI)A possible future AI that could learn almost any mental task a human can; it doesn't exist yet.
  • Red teamingTesting an AI by trying hard, on purpose, to make it fail or misbehave, so the problems can be fixed.
  • AI alignmentMaking sure an AI tries to do what people really intend and value, not just what they literally said.
  • EU AI ActThe European Union's law on artificial intelligence, adopted in 2024 and often called the world's first broad AI law.
  • ProxyA piece of data that indirectly gives away something else, so a model can learn a bias it was never shown directly.
  • Filter bubbleWhen recommendation algorithms keep showing you more of what you already like or believe, so you rarely see anything else.
  • AI watermarkA hidden or visible mark added to AI-made pictures, audio, video or text to show that AI created them.
